phase1.intro:
try-catch-finally is the actual mechanism for catching an exception once it happens, rather than just letting it crash the program.

Where do you want to start?

topics.buttonText: How does try and catch actually work?
dialogue: Code that might go wrong lives inside the [[term:try]] block. The moment something inside it throws, Java immediately jumps out of the rest of the try block and looks for a matching [[term:catch]] — it jumps the instant the exception fires.

[[warn:Order matters — Java checks catch blocks top to bottom and uses the FIRST one that matches]]. [[key:Specific exception types have to come before more general ones]], or the general catch swallows it first.

stickyNote.flavor: 🎯 first matching catch wins, top to bottom
stickyNote.definition: Code that might throw lives in try; matching catch blocks are checked top-to-bottom, so specific types must come before general ones.

topics.buttonText: What makes finally different from catch?
dialogue: The [[term:finally]] block runs no matter what — whether the try block succeeded, an exception got caught, or even if the catch block itself threw something new. That makes it the right place for cleanup that absolutely has to happen either way, like closing a file.

stickyNote.definition: finally runs regardless of what happened in try or catch — the right place for cleanup like closing files or connections.

topics.buttonText: Can a try block just stand alone?
dialogue: [[key:A try block needs at least a catch or a finally (or both) — it can't stand alone]]. Java won't let you write risky code without some plan for what happens if it goes wrong.

stickyNote.flavor: 📏 needs a catch or a finally, no exceptions
stickyNote.definition: A try block must be followed by at least one catch or a finally block — it cannot exist on its own.

phase1.openingDialogue: try holds risky code, catch handles it when it fails, and finally always runs — the actual mechanism for surviving an exception. 🛠️

phase2.errorMessage:
TryCatchExample.java:12: error: exception ArithmeticException has already been caught
        catch (ArithmeticException e) {  // Unreachable!
        ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
You stacked catch (Exception e) BEFORE catch (ArithmeticException e) — and since Exception is the parent of every exception type, including ArithmeticException, that first catch block would swallow an ArithmeticException before the second one ever gets a chance to run.

[[warn:Java actually catches this at compile time, not runtime]] — it can tell statically that the second catch block is unreachable dead code, and refuses to build rather than let you ship a catch block that can never fire.

[[key:the fix is always the same shape: order catch blocks from most specific to most general]], ending with the broadest type (usually Exception) last, as a genuine catch-all for anything you didn't specifically plan for.
phase2.openingDialogue: Watch what happens when a general catch jumps the line~

phase3.openingDialogue: Let's build a safety net around risky code~

mcq.question:
Which statement about try-catch-finally is TRUE?

A) A try block can exist without any catch or finally block
B) catch blocks should be ordered from most general to most specific
C) The finally block runs even if the try block completes with no exception
D) Only one catch block is allowed per try block

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates a Scanner for user input
2. In try block: asks for two numbers and divides first by second
3. Catches ArithmeticException (division by zero)
4. Catches Exception (for any other error)
5. Has finally block that prints "Operation complete"

Test it with both valid and invalid inputs.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: finally blocks run so reliably that they can even execute after a return statement inside try or catch — and if a finally block also contains its own return, it actually overrides the earlier one. That surprising edge case is exactly why most style guides recommend never putting a return inside finally at all.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thought before you go~
